title: “MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE”: Biblical Passion That Money Cannot Buy
paragraphs: “MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE”: Biblical Passion That Money Cannot Buy
You can drown almost anything if the water rises high enough. But Scripture says there is a kind of love that can go under the flood—and come back burning.
There are some things money can buy.
A beautiful house.
A carefully chosen gift.
A plane ticket across the world.
Flowers delivered to a doorstep.
A wedding that leaves everyone speechless.
A comfortable bed.
A table overflowing with food.
Even the appearance of a perfect life.
But there is something money has never been able to purchase.
Love.
Not the kind that poses for photographs.
Not the kind that survives only while everything feels good.
Not attraction dressed up as covenant.
Not obsession mistaken for devotion.
Not affection that remains only until suffering arrives.
Real love.
The kind that walks through fire.
The kind that gets wounded and refuses to become counterfeit.
The kind that cannot be auctioned to the highest bidder.
The kind that remains when the gifts disappear, the applause stops, beauty changes, money runs low, and life becomes painfully different from what you imagined.
Thousands of years ago, Scripture described that love with an image so violent and beautiful that it still reaches into the human heart:
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it…”
Song of Songs 8:7.
But the Hebrew carries something worth slowing down long enough to hear.
מַיִם רַבִּים לֹא יוּכְלוּ לְכַבּוֹת אֶת־הָאַהֲבָה
Mayim rabbim lo yukhelu lekhabbot et-ha’ahavah.
“Many waters are not able to extinguish love.”
Then:
וּנְהָרוֹת לֹא יִשְׁטְפוּהָ
Uneharot lo yishtefuha.
“Nor can rivers sweep it away.”
And then comes the line that destroys one of humanity’s oldest illusions:
אִם־יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶת־כָּל־הוֹן בֵּיתוֹ בָּאַהֲבָה בּוֹז יָבוּזוּ לוֹ
Even if a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly despised.
Read that again.
All the wealth of his house.
Everything.
And still he cannot buy love.
That is the scandal.
And perhaps somewhere inside that sentence is your story.
Because maybe you have spent years trying to purchase with performance what can only be received through love.
Maybe you learned early that affection came when you behaved.
Approval came when you succeeded.
Attention came when you looked attractive.
Praise came when you accomplished something.
Acceptance came when you were useful.
So you became useful.
Very useful.
You learned how to smile while exhausted.
How to serve while empty.
How to say, “I’m okay,” while something inside you was quietly collapsing.
You learned how to give people what they wanted because somewhere deep inside, you were terrified that if you stopped performing, they might stop loving you.
And eventually that way of thinking entered your relationship with God.
You may never have said it aloud.
But you started bargaining.
“God, if I become better…”
“If I pray more…”
“If I serve harder…”
“If I stop struggling…”
“If I become the Christian everyone thinks I should be…”
“Maybe then You will really love me.”
And that is where the Gospel walks into the room and overturns the table.
Because the Gospel does not announce that sinful people finally became lovable enough for God.
It announces something infinitely more astonishing.
God loved us while we were still sinners.
Romans 5:8 does not say Christ waited for humanity to become impressive.
It says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after every secret was confessed.
Not after every relationship was repaired.
Not after the shame stopped screaming.
Not after we became religious enough to deserve Him.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not make sin insignificant.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Yet God’s grace is so astonishing that the price was not placed into our hands.
Christ bore it.
This is where we must understand Song of Songs carefully.

Song of Songs is first and directly poetry celebrating human love, desire, covenant affection, longing, and marital devotion. We should not erase that meaning by pretending every romantic line is secretly an allegory with no concern for human marriage.
But neither should Christians read Scripture with Christ absent from the horizon.
The love celebrated in marriage points us toward something larger because throughout the New Testament marriage itself becomes a profound picture of Christ and His people.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:25:
There it is again.
Love gives.
But notice the difference between giving because you love and giving to purchase love.
That difference changes everything.
Song of Songs says wealth cannot purchase love.
The Gospel says Christ loved—and therefore gave Himself.
Christian generosity works the same way.
We do not give so God will love us.
We give because in Christ we have encountered a love we could never purchase.
We do not obey to make Jesus die for us.
He already died.
We do not repent so we can become valuable enough for the Savior.
We repent because the Savior is worthy, sin is deadly, and grace has opened the way home.
We do not surrender because surrender purchases salvation.
Salvation is the gift that finally teaches us why surrender is worth it.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this needs to hear tonight.
You cannot buy what Jesus offers freely.
You cannot out-donate your guilt.
You cannot out-serve your shame.
You cannot perform your way into adoption.
You cannot impress the Father into calling you His child.
You cannot make the blood of Christ more effective by adding your achievements to it.
You come empty-handed.
That is humiliating to pride.
And breathtaking to the exhausted.
Because empty hands are exactly the hands capable of receiving a gift.
Maybe your life has been one long attempt to prove you are worth loving.
Jesus is not asking you to audition.
He is calling you to repent, believe, and come home.
And some of us desperately need to distinguish biblical love from the counterfeit version our culture often sells.
Biblical love is not merely intensity.
Intensity can disappear tomorrow.
Biblical love is not possession.
Jealous control can call itself love while slowly suffocating another human being.
Biblical love is not lust.
Lust asks, “What can I take from you?”
Love asks, “How can I seek your genuine good?”
Biblical love is not tolerating everything another person does.
Sometimes love confronts.
Sometimes love tells the truth.
Sometimes love establishes boundaries.
Sometimes love refuses to participate in destruction.
Sometimes love says the painful thing precisely because silence would be easier.

And love is not proved by remaining in danger. Song of Songs should never be weaponized to tell an abused person that “many waters cannot quench love,” therefore they must silently endure violence or coercion. Biblical love does not require pretending evil is good.
Love rejoices in truth.
And real love survives truth.
That may be why some relationships collapse the moment honesty enters the room.
They were being held together by performance.
Not love.
But imagine being completely known and still genuinely loved.
That is one of the deepest longings inside the human heart.
We hide because we fear that if people knew everything, they would leave.
We edit ourselves.
Crop the photograph.
Delete the history.
Hide the messages.
Cover the scars.
Change the subject.
Raise our hands during worship while secretly wondering whether God is disgusted with the person underneath them.
Then the Gospel does something terrifying.
It turns on the light.
And something beautiful happens.
Jesus does not expose darkness merely to humiliate sinners.
He brings darkness into the light so sinners can be forgiven, cleansed, restored, and transformed.
Grace is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
Grace is God dealing with sin at the cross so completely that the sinner who trusts in Christ can stop hiding behind excuses and finally confess the truth.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is one of grace’s beautiful consequences.
You stop defending the prison once you realize the door has been opened.
You stop decorating the chains.
You stop renaming bondage.
You finally say:
“Jesus, this is me.”
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the Sunday version.
Me.
The angry me.
The jealous me.
The lustful me.
The frightened me.
The addicted me.
The bitter me.
The hypocritical me.
The wounded me.
The one who knew better and still did it.
The one who promised You, “Never again,” and somehow ended up there again.
And Christianity makes an outrageous announcement to that person:
There is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Cross-shaped grace.
Resurrection-confirmed grace.
Grace that forgives you and then refuses to leave you enslaved to what was destroying you.
Because Jesus does not merely rewrite reputations.
He transforms people.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Think about Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then fear entered the room.
Three times he denied knowing Jesus.
Imagine carrying that memory.
The sound of your own voice denying the One you claimed you would die for.
Then the rooster.
Then the realization.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
What do you do when the person who betrayed Jesus is you?
John 21 gives us one of Scripture’s most tender scenes.
The resurrected Christ meets Peter again.
There is breakfast.
There is conversation.
There is restoration.
Jesus does not pretend Peter never failed.
But neither does Peter’s failure receive authority to write the final chapter of Peter’s life.
That authority belongs to Jesus.
Peter’s scandal was real.
Grace was more powerful.
Maybe yours is real too.
Maybe you have destroyed trust.
Maybe you have been carrying something you hope nobody ever discovers.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out something inside you.
Maybe resentment has lived in your heart so long that you no longer remember who you were before it moved in.
Maybe you walked away from God.
Maybe church hurt became the doorway through which you quietly abandoned prayer.
Maybe you still attend church physically, but spiritually you have been gone for years.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong because nobody knows how tired you actually are.
Listen.
The answer is not pretending harder.
Come to Christ.
Not merely to religious activity.
Christ.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who ate with people respectable society despised.
The One who confronted self-righteousness.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who carried a cross.
The One who died.
The One who was buried.
The One who rose.
The One who still saves.
And when the waters rise—and they will—remember the image Scripture gave us.
Many waters cannot quench love.
There will be waters.
Marriage discovers this.
Friendship discovers this.
Parenthood discovers this.
Discipleship discovers this.
There are hospital waters.
Funeral waters.
Betrayal waters.
Financial waters.
Temptation waters.
Depression and grief.
Long nights.
Unanswered questions.
Prodigal children.
Broken promises.
Aging bodies.
Empty chairs.
Prayers whose answers did not arrive in the form you expected.
Faith is not the promise that Christians will never enter deep water.
Sometimes faith sounds like Isaiah 43:2:
“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee.”
Not if.
When.
And Christianity ultimately anchors hope not in the strength of our emotional passion for God, but in God’s faithfulness and the finished work of Christ.
Your emotions fluctuate.
His character does not.
Your grip sometimes weakens.
His promises do not become untrue because your hands are trembling.
This is why Christian love cannot finally be reduced to butterflies, goosebumps, worship music, romantic feelings, or inspirational moments.
Love becomes visible in faithfulness.
In forgiveness.
In truth.
In sacrifice.
In repentance.
In staying when staying is righteous.
In leaving sin when sin has become familiar.
In confessing when hiding would preserve your reputation.
In giving without trying to purchase applause.
In serving when nobody knows your name.
In choosing Christ when compromise would be easier.
And that brings us back to money.
“If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.”
Love cannot be bought.
And that truth must govern Christian ministry too.
It does not.
A donation is not forgiveness.
Buying a Christian book does not make someone righteous.
Supporting a ministry does not force God to bless you.
And no faithful Christian ministry should manipulate you into believing otherwise.
Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Your place in the family of God cannot be purchased.
But there is another biblical truth.
Grace produces generosity.
The New Testament repeatedly shows believers voluntarily supporting Gospel work, caring for those in need, and sharing material resources so ministry can continue.
Paul describes Christian giving in 2 Corinthians 9:7 with extraordinary clarity:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
That matters.

So if Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, brought Scripture into a dark season, helped you return to Jesus, encouraged you when you wanted to quit, or given you something worth sending to another struggling soul, you can help this work continue.
Not because giving money earns heaven.
But because voluntary generosity can put resources behind work you believe is worth continuing.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you want to help.
Never because you think God is selling His affection.
He is not.
And there is another way to help that may cost you nothing.
One share can put the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
You do not know who is awake at 2:13 in the morning scrolling through Facebook because their marriage is collapsing.
You do not know who is sitting alone wondering whether God could forgive what they have done.
You do not know which old friend is silently losing a battle nobody knows exists.
You do not know which unbelieving relative has rejected church but might still read an article you shared because they trust you.
Not for numbers.
For people.
And if you have watched Jesus patiently restore pieces of your life you thought were permanently ruined, tell somebody what He has done.
Your testimony might become another person’s reason to believe that their story is not finished.
Because eventually the waters rise.
And when they do, you may need to come back and remember:
Love is not proved by how much money someone spends.
Love is not proved by how impressive someone looks.
Love is not proved by emotion alone.
Love has weight.
Love has truth.
Love has faithfulness.
And at the center of the Christian story stands a cross where love was not purchased by us but demonstrated toward us.
Jesus did not come because humanity finally became worthy.
He came because sinners needed a Savior.
He did not die because sin was trivial.
He died because sin was deadly.
He did not rise merely to make bad people slightly nicer.
He rose victorious, and everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith receives a new identity, a new hope, and ultimately the promise of resurrection life.
That is why the Gospel is bigger than inspiration.
It is rescue.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person drifting from God.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Let them encounter the Word.
Use them.
Share them.
Study.
Test what you read against Scripture.
Grow.
And wherever truth confronts you, do not merely admire it.
Respond to it.
Because someday all the things we thought made us valuable will fall from our hands.
The money.
The accomplishments.
The titles.
The followers.
The possessions.
The carefully maintained image.
None of it can purchase the thing our souls need most.
But Jesus has already done what money could never do.
The question is not whether you can afford Him.
You cannot buy Him.
The question is whether you will stop trying to save yourself and receive the mercy you could never earn.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come into the light.
Let Christ begin transforming what shame told you must remain hidden forever.
Because the goal was never merely to build an audience.
The goal is to point human beings toward Jesus.
There are still people drowning beneath waters nobody else can see.
And they need to know there is a love money cannot purchase, suffering cannot cheaply imitate, and death itself could not hold in the grave.
When every counterfeit love has named its price, the scarred hands of Jesus will still be telling you that grace was never for sale.
